archetype.name: Rebuilding (outshot nightly)
archetype.definition: A team coming off two bottom-three finishes that still loses the puck and the chances in most games, so the record depends on whether its goalies or shooters can cover a structural gap.

report.headline: Chicago's 3-6 start is honest: the shot share, not luck, is the problem.
report.take:
Chicago opens its third straight rebuilding season looking like the team from the last two. It finished 31st and 30th on the site in those years, with 61 and then 72 standings points. This start is no better. At 3-6-0 the Blackhawks sit last in the Central and 30th on the site, and the goal margin is worse than either of those seasons: -1.67 a game, 29th in the league. Carried over 82 games, that is a 55-point pace, which would be a step back from last year.

The cause is territorial. Chicago has 40.4% of the 5-on-5 expected goals (30th) and 42% of the shot attempts (29th). It takes 21.4 shots a game against a league norm of 27.2 and allows 30.3. Those shares are lower than the 43.1% and 42.4% xGF it posted in the two previous seasons, so the play-driving hole has grown, not closed. The pressure falls hardest on the defense. Opposing defensemen are scoring 1.3 points a game above their own averages against Chicago (31st), and they account for 30.3% of the points against it, compared with a league share of 24.2%. That points to point shots and pinches going unpunished, which you see when a team can't get out of its own zone.

The numbers say this is not a bad-luck story. The skaters shoot 10.9%, close to the league's 11.3%, so the offense isn't being robbed. The team sits 11th in Pts vs Goal Diff, so it has, if anything, squeezed a little extra out of close games, including the overtime win over Winnipeg. The one real drag beyond process is goaltending: .875 team save percentage and -4.4 GSAx. Last season the Blackhawks had +7.5 GSAx, and that cushion is what made a 42% expected-goals team look like a 72-point team. Without it, the gap shows in the scoreline.

Where it heads depends on whether Spencer Knight steadies things and whether the top of the lineup stops getting buried. Patrick Kane is -11 with a 35.1% xGF, and Anton Frondell is at 34.7%. Meanwhile the third and fourth lines of Ryan Greene, Jordan Greenway and Cole Smith are near break-even. Some save-percentage recovery is likely and would lift the points pace. The shot share is the real ceiling, though, and nothing in nine games suggests it is about to rise to respectability.

strengths.title: Depth forwards breaking even
strengths.body: The low-minute forwards are the only group Chicago isn't getting outplayed with. Ryan Greene is at 51.3% xGF, Jordan Greenway 49.8% and Cole Smith 48.8%, all while the top six sit well below 40%. That reflects sheltered usage as much as quality, but it gives the coach a set of shifts he can trust. It probably lasts, because those players' roles won't change much.

strengths.title: Finishing is not the problem
strengths.body: Chicago's skaters convert at a league-normal rate: 10.9% shooting, 17th, against a league average of 11.3%. Frank Nazar and Roman Kantserov have three goals apiece. The offense is low because the volume isn't there, not because the shooters are cold. That means there is no hidden collapse coming, and any gains in shot volume should turn into goals.

strengths.title: Levshunov steadies the blueline
strengths.body: Artyom Levshunov, playing 20.45 minutes, ranks 46th of 242 on the defense tab. No other Chicago defenseman cracks the top 110. He is the one defenseman worth building pairings around, and his ranking stands out on a group graded D-.

concerns.title: Losing the territory every night
concerns.body: Chicago has 40.4% of expected goals and 42% of shot attempts at 5-on-5, both bottom-three. It is outshot by a wide margin: 5.8 fewer shots for and 4 more against per game than the league norm. Both shares are below the already-poor levels of the last two seasons. This is a structural issue that shouldn't be written off as early-season noise.

concerns.title: No goaltending cushion this year
concerns.body: Last season's +7.5 GSAx masked a 42% expected-goals team. This year the goalies are at -4.4 and a .875 save percentage, 26th. Knight has been close to average at -1 GSAx. Soderblom's two starts at .820 did most of the damage, so a return to Knight as the clear starter should help at the margin.

concerns.title: Top line and special teams buried
concerns.body: Kane is -11 with a 35.1% xGF on 19.45 minutes a night, and Frondell is at 34.7%. The minutes going to the most-used forwards are the worst minutes on the team. The power play is at 12.5% (28th) and the penalty kill at 74.1% (23rd), so neither unit claws anything back.

trend.note: The last five games at 2-3-0, a .400 points percentage, are barely better than the season as a whole, still allowing 3.8 goals a game. The two home wins over Pittsburgh and Winnipeg were followed by a 4-0 loss to Dallas.

weekAhead.headline: Three home games: two winnable, one stiff test vs Florida
weekAhead.body:
All three games are at home, and the slate splits cleanly. Montréal (4-3-1, 20th on the site) and Los Angeles (0-4-2, 31st) both carry goaltending problems: save percentages of .868 and .861, among the worst in the league. Florida (5-2-2, 6th) is the opposite: B+ grades across the roster and a 58% shot-attempt share, third in the league.

The trap is that both weaker opponents push play. Montréal has 54.3% xGF and Los Angeles takes 29.8 shots a game, eighth. A team that allows 30.3 shots won't win these on territory. The path is to finish on the few chances it gets against shaky goalies, and in the Kings' case to cash in on a power play facing the league's 31st-ranked penalty kill. Two points out of these three games would be par, and four would be a good week.

keyMatchups.title: Power play vs Kings' leaky kill
keyMatchups.body: Los Angeles kills just 61.9% of penalties, 31st, and Chicago's 12.5% power play has nowhere easier to get going. The Kings also carry -9 GSAx. A special-teams goal or two may be the margin in a game Chicago will probably lose on shots.

keyMatchups.title: Florida's puck possession
keyMatchups.body: Florida holds 58% of shot attempts and allows only 23.9 shots a game. Its defense is holding wingers and defensemen under their averages, at 7th and 5th. Against a Chicago team that takes 21.4 shots a game, this sets up as a long night in its own zone unless Knight steals it.

keyMatchups.title: Two weak goaltending tandems
keyMatchups.body: Montréal's goaltending is graded D+ with a .868 save percentage, and the Kings' .861 is 30th. Chicago's shooters convert at a league-normal rate, so the few looks they get have a better chance of going in than usual.

weekAhead.watch: Shots against: if Chicago can keep Montréal and Los Angeles near the league norm instead of 30-plus, the goaltending matchups favor it.

restOfSeason.body:
The likely path is a modest recovery toward last season's level, not beyond it. Goaltending should stabilize from -4.4 GSAx as Knight takes the starts, and a .875 save percentage is unlikely to hold over 73 more games. That alone should push the points pace up from 55. The 5-on-5 shares, though, are the real signal, and they are worse than in either of the last two seasons. This team needed +7.5 GSAx to reach 72 points a year ago.

Expect something in the range of 58 to 68 standings points and goals against settling around 3.5 a game. Shooting luck is neutral and close-game luck slightly positive, so there is no hidden upside on the scoreboard. Upside would have to come from the top forwards and the second and third defense pairings improving their shot shares.
swingFactors: Knight's save percentage over a full workload
Top-six forwards' shot share, led by Kane and Frondell
Power play climbing toward league average

confidence.note: Only nine games played, but the shot and expected-goal shares match two prior seasons of history.
